The general public is also really bad at understanding the difference between broad "homelessness" and chronic homelessness. The vast majority of people counted as homeless are essentially invisible to the general population because they live in temporary housing, are staying with loved ones, or use shelters. The people on the street that cause (and have!) the most safety concerns are more often chronically homeless; a combination of their own agency and financial/mental health/addiction issues make being unhoused their perceived best option. I have worked with unhoused people for a long time and many chronically unhoused people have made clear to me that this is the life they're choosing, maybe out of desperation, but nevertheless. It’s exciting that we have the prospect of learning so much more about the universe and so quickly!  If we find them, we won’t ever be able to visit worlds with their own life most likely, but just knowing they are there, knowing we are part of a normal larger process that happens elsewhere, and finding out how to monitor them could have profound psychic effects on humanity, I suspect.  And remember earth was habitable, but without oxygen for a long time, so chances of a new Eden are awfully slim!

One of the key things is to find which of the super earths have, like earth, a magnetic field to protect their atmospheres from being stripped away and to protect any life there from hard stellar radiation.  A recent model suggests that a super earth in the 3x to 6x earth mass range could have a mantle dynamo caused by internal pressures instead of by a radioactive core like ours.  That would be huge.  It would be good to be able to look for magnetic fields directly.  

Tectonic dynamics might also be critical to life formation, and that could come with the convecting mantle dynamos that large super earths might have.  Tectonic activity also increases the likelihood of continents forming as lighter material cycles out of the mantle and accretes at subduction zones.  In warm shallow oceans without continents, perhaps at best you only end up with vast fields of microbial mats and associated microorganisms, as in the “boring billion” of the history of life on earth.

Also, AI works because human beings had new concepts and ideas over the centuries that were used to train AI. So, if we now stop having new concepts and ideas, how the heck does that work as time goes on? I guess the evolution of human knowledge will pretty much end over the next several years and our current slow decline will devolve into a fast one and hasten the end of civilization, aided by AI all the way to the bottom.

Namely, that law is not, nor ever written and enforced for all, but rather, law is ultimately controlled and shaped by a select few, a powerful few. In our time, a wealthy few. And as such, the law looses it mores to truth and dignity. The modern world has yet to register how the enlightenment with its values of truth and humanism was exchanged for a false idealism, the 'isms' of a perfectable future. It turns out that just as worse as the immediate horrors of a belief in culture (Fascism) or the state (Communism), is the long-term destructiveness of the market (Capitalism). SIDE NOTE: Hacking aside, in a world of limited physical resources, this seems like a no-brainer. Especially since it's a standard most companies once held themselves to, so we know it can be done. “Polarization” implies a kind of equivalence, in this instance, a false equivalence between “right” and “left.” Instead of polarization, we are living through an age of right-wing reaction, triggered by the gains made by historically excluded groups: Black people, women, LGBTQ people and those with disabilities.
It is  hardly a coincidence that Trump's targets and scapegoats   are those same groups .
 Exactly 100 years ago, the philosopher Alfred North Whitehead said, “It is the first step in sociological wisdom, to recognize, that the major advances in civilization are processes which all but wreck the societies in which they occur.” In complimenting Whitehead, Albert O. Hirschman, ("The Rhetoric of Reaction"), says he would have left out the “all but,” 
Racial bigotry, misogyny and homophobia have also provided the shiny objects that keep us from focusing on America’s world class inequality: a tiny sliver of super-rich people, another sliver of rich ones, declining and increasingly insecure middle and working classes and entrenched poverty. Which, as historian Walter Scheidel points out ("The Great Leveler") has rarely ended peacefully. 
Finally, there is the far-right strategy of destroying trust in our institutions as the pathway to undermining liberal democracy. ("Democracy in Chains," Nancy Maclean), a smashing success that has paved the way to Trump and his crew. 
Conclusion: we are in far deeper trouble and face greater dangers than this column implies.

comments.name: FFlavius
comments.body:
Watching from Europe, where we see similar trends: before reaching for sociology and psychology, let’s go to the root. We are an animal species, driven by instincts that culture usually keeps in check. Which animal should we study? I’d suggest pigs, and not only because Orwell made them the protagonists of Animal Farm. My father’s farm raised some 6,000 pigs a year, and I was struck by how much their behavior resembled ours (or is it the other way around?). A group of pigs always has a dominant animal. Divide the pen with a low partition, and soon there are two, one on each side, each surrounded by its closest followers. The two then bite each other across the partition, without ever climbing over it. On both sides the pattern is the same: when the dominant pig attacks a weaker one, it isn’t the one that finishes it off. Its followers do.

Researchers know that the worst of these behaviors flare up under crowding, stress and barren surroundings, and that tail biting is not seen in wild boars. Even the “alpha wolf” was a product of captivity: the scientist who popularized it later retracted the idea, finding that wild packs are simply families. So the question isn’t whether “the beast” lives within us, but which barriers have broken down, and what conditions we’ve created, to let it resurface.

comments.name: William
comments.body:
“Letters to the Editor” is the second thing I read in the morning (after looking at the front page).  The conversation is always wide-ranging.  And it’s good to be part of it!  On-line comments are different.  Yes there is some moderation of those comments; but a letter to the editor is on a different plane.   It has to be short, clear, and direct.  The discipline of writing one is like turning out a haiku.  

The collection of letters appended to the column show how varied are the themes and contributors that make up this part of The NYT.

comments.name: BeDoHave

comments.name: Gowan McAvity
comments.body: I wrote a comment that wasn’t published before the section closed, so I emailed it to the editors and author telling them that and that Maureen Dowd, the author, might enjoy the comment. Ms. Dowd replied directly saying she couldn’t believe it didn’t run. Tom Feyer then emailed telling me it was a wonderful letter would I like to publish or was it just a message for Maureen?. He offer to edit and send a playback. Of course, I accepted and gave permission to publish. We went back and forth and Mr. Feyer later kindly let me know when the letter was published. I went to the corner mart to pick up a print copy. It was a thrilling and surreal exchange. I was sitting alone on my porch on a sunny morning reading the Saturday paper and suddenly I was corresponding with the Maureen Dowd and Tom Feyer was asking if his edit was satisfactory. The print copy is framed and on the office wall.

comments.name: Larry

I love all the people on here saying how coaching is a scam despite a large amount of scientific evidence that it can be very helpful and for some even life changing. There are bad doctors, and bad therapists, and we don’t call those a scam. 

I think coaching fills a really important void left by failing social structures, a move away from religions, and a desire most people have to become a more fully realized version of themselves. 

$500 I’d actually fairly cheap for a coach depending on what kind of coaching you get and big companies invest hundreds of thousands of dollars in coaching. And really good therapists and doctors learn and use coaching techniques. 

There are many ways to get support and coaching is a great one but it’s not the only one. If it works great! If not keep searching for what’s right for you.

comments.name: GN
comments.body:
Predictably, there are a lot of negative comments here.

Because life coaching is unregulated, its practitioners- and its pricing- vary widely. There are advantages and disadvantages to this; the main thing is, you can find a coach that works for you. Everyone’s approaches are different and what works for one client won’t work for another. 

Unfortunately many people still resist getting therapy because of the stigma of mental health treatment, or due to lack of access or funds. Life coaching can coax these hesitant individuals into seeking support. 

I should know- I was one of them. I was struggling in my 20s but didn’t want to do therapy because I naively assumed I already knew what the therapist would say. A friend of a relative was completing her LC training and offered me free sessions so she could reach the required coaching hours to receive her certificate. She was so positive, warm, and understanding. She was a mentor who helped me reframe my way of thinking and recognize my strengths. 

So, I wouldn’t be so quick to judge life coaches… aside from the ones charging $500 an hour :)

Appreciate what this review is trying to do, but it's all artifice. Music either grabs and moves you or it doesn't. Whatever intellectual scaffolding you can attach to it is ultimately in service to what and how it made you feel. The question I kept circling around isn't, "Is Cameron Winter Serious?" but "Do New York Times music critics know how to enjoy themselves?" (Surely, they can. I cannot explain away Jon Caramanica's horrendous taste in pop music without surrendering to idea that he enjoys it and how it makes him feel. But the question remains for Zoladz and her friends.)

Of course Cameron Winter's serious. Of course he isn't playing a joke on people. And what's so absurd about picking up a guitar or a piano and trying to write a great rock song in the first place? Mozart never composed anything on the piano more moving and perfect than Bach, but what a loss for the world if he just threw up his hands and said, "The best has already been written!"

comments.name: Goodrune
comments.body:
I am German, I lived and worked in the U.S. for 10 years and I am a member of a German student fraternity. Here, they have a tradition going back to the 1700s, mainly as a congregation of students who came from the same geographical area. Today, some have religious backgrounds, political beliefs, some are "fencing", others aren't. Mine is a fencing fraternity ("Corps") and I can say that shedding blood or at least risking it, creates a tight bond. It is a tightly regulated ritual. Neither professional networking is the main driver to join, nor excessive parties. They are abundant elsewhere.
I believe the author forgot a very U.S.-specific point: Kids grow up in a an overly protected environment, helicoptering parents have 24/7 surveillance on their offspring. They run tracking and spy-apps on their cell phones and make sure they are always "safe". Then - bang - they move to a college town 1000 miles away. Fraternities offer a well-organized party life, but also cost an "arm and a leg". The kids want something in return. Alcohol and drugs are the experience-booster, which are finally legal to consume. They can catch up with all the parties they have missed so far. That is the fertile ground - not the only reason, but heavily contributing.
Based on what is publicly known about the Cornell case, I can see "Jane Doe" and the frat members being carried away under their substance influence. The real scandal for me are the sober members of the chat group who just let it happen.

comments.body:
An article in the British media written by a British university student who had spent a year at an American university pointed out the importance of access to alcohol in recruiting students to frats and sororities, as most students' only option for getting alcohol because they are under 21.  The older members buy alcohol for the younger members and hold large, alcohol-fuelled parties that many of both sexes want to attend. 

 In other countries, the legal drinking age is 18 or even 16, and students typically go out to a pub, a club or the equivalent, where there are older adults to oversee alcohol consumption, or a small group of friends living together will drink together at their dorm or house. I was a member of the team that renegotiated the Panguna mining agreement on behalf of the newly self-governing Papua New Guinea government in 1974, working with then-Chief Minister Michael Somare and the Bougainvilleans John Momis (then chair of the Constitutional Planning Committee and later Governor and President of Bougainville) and Paul Lapun, then PNG Minister for Mines. To our credit, we ended a tax regime, dictated in 1967 to then-colony PNG by the colonial power Australia, that basically gave away the natural resources for the first 20 years of the mine's life, and introduced a novel and effective "resource-rernt" taxation regime that captured most of the excess profits for the national government. 
   What we failed to do, however, despite the input of Momis and Lapun, was to adequately take into account the needs of the people who lived near the mine—at the time, it was the world's second-largest open-pit mining operation. And we failed to anticipate the cumulative effect, over the two decades between our renegotiation of the agreement and the outbreak of rebellion on Bougainville in the 1990s, of the huge changes to the local environment that would be wrought by the mining operations. Victoria Kim's reporting, and the accompanying photographs, brings that effect into focus. I fear, however, that the new Bougainville government, moving ahead quickly with an obscure corporate partner, will simply repeat our earlier mistakes. Mi sori tumas.

In all seriousness, we know what goes wrong from living on or in mine waste. There are so many examples, worldwide. Leaching heavy metals, acid mine drainage, mudslides or flooding, even something as simple as toxic dust. Not only is living near the tailings a hazard, these people also seem to be living near/occupying major components of the mine that will have to be vacated in order to operate again. Living near the drainage tunnel, in the pit, or on any of the tailings is asking for any number of life-altering conditions (cancers, disorders, floods, mudslides). I have significant doubts that this very small, somewhat unknown company will have human and environmental concerns anywhere near the top of the list when reopening the mine.

comments.name: Critique
comments.body: Today's youth, are growing up in a world where social media, movies, and consumer culture constantly showcase glamorous lifestyles, luxury brands, expensive gadgets, and seemingly effortless success. While ambition, material aspirations, and the desire for a better life are natural and often positive forces, the relentless exposure to carefully curated images can create unrealistic expectations about wealth and success. What is frequently missing from these portrayals is the hard work, patience, discipline, and sometimes sheer luck required to achieve financial prosperity. For some young people, the pressure to keep up with their peers or social media idols can lead to poor financial decisions, risky employment opportunities, migration under difficult or exploitative conditions, and, in extreme cases, even illegal activities. Of course, many young people pursue their ambitions responsibly, and economic pressures and limited opportunities also play a significant role in the choices they make. The real concern is not ambition or the desire for material comforts, but a culture that increasingly celebrates the appearance of success over the effort, integrity, and perseverance needed to achieve it.

I never had bunions until after dropping a can of shaving creme and the bottom edge coming down like a guilloutine on my big toe joint, cutting the skin and causing bruise. Once the bruising reduced, I had almost no movement' the joint was stiff. It was painful to walk and flex joint. It effected my walking gait. Up until this injury, I typically hiked and walked about 15 miles per week and practiced yoga daily on top of normal work and other activities, so this was very disruptive. 

Immediately, I started investigating and trying alternatives to heal. Podiatrist recommended surgery. Yet, when asked about likely outcome, podiatrist explained degree of movement possible would be no better than I had with the injury. Second podiatrist gave an orthodic insert that created space for the big toe to drop down. Using YogaToes helped a bit. I sought a chiropractor who works on extremities and after several months was referred to a Chiropractor who uses the Gonstead method. By then, a bunion had developed and the joint was arthritic with calcification. The Gonstead Chiropractor massaged the fascia and manipulated the toe gently in a way that achieved movement in the joint that I had not been able to do myself initially. Regular manipulations and wearing the orthodic helped ... after approximately 6 months much of the calcification was gone, pain gone, movement nearer to normal, and bunion much reduced and barely noticeable.

She claimed the surgery was non-invasive and had a fast heal time. I asked her if surgery was really necessary, or if we could try other measures.  She insisted surgery was necessary. It is near impossible to get medical appointments where I live (it took me months to see her), so I didn't get a second opinion.  She put me in a boot after the surgery and told me I could walk right away. I ended up with 4 fractures in my foot because she told me I could put weight on the foot.  So she did a second surgery to undo the bunion surgery to fix the fractures.  I couldn't walk for 3 months. One year later and my foot is much worse than it was a year ago.  I wish I had never had the surgery.  She is an experienced foot surgeon who has a very good reputation. However, in hindsight I now realize that she pushed the surgery when she shouldn't have - and she was irresponsible in letting me walk right after the surgery.  Now she wants to do MORE surgery to fix my foot.  No way.  If my foot gets unbearable I'll find a different foot surgeon.

Seaweed picks up heavy metals and other pollutants so origin matters (I try to avoid Chinese harvested).  Fish is worse that way, though, and seaweed portion size is usually much smaller anyway.  Also, good brands do careful sorting and rinsing (as you'll find out as you use it).

Wakame is a staple spice/condiment my diet.  It's mild, a light touch in dishes other seaweed would dominate.  It's relatively low in iodine (i.e. not an overload).  It's also particularly high in polysaccharides like fucoidan (a water soluble fiber which has promise as an antinflammatory and immune booster).  I add it to soups, steamed greens, rolled omelets, and my improvised variable veggie burger recipe for chewy bite and umami flavor.

I had the good fortune to co-lead a youth delegation to Ukraine in the summer of 1992. The mood there was palpably optimistic, as this great people felt they'd finally lifted the yolk of Russian oppression. Little did we know then that a dictator would rise in Russia as malevolent as those in the Soviet Union. Nor could I have fathomed an American president be in league with the leader of our former Cold War adversary. The ocean for many is out of sight and mind. But Atlantic fish stocks 10 years ago were between 1/1,000 and 1/10,000 of what they were just 150 to 200 years ago. (1) 

The continental shelves used to be forests of sponges and corals, critical habitat for fish development.

Trawling has reduced to mud, to parking lot, a greater area of the ocean floor than the area of forests cut down in the history of humanity.

Over hunting and fishing, habitat loss, invasive species, pollution and now climate change.

None of these things happen in a vacuum, but there are synergies among them which make the whole vastly greater than the sum of the parts.

We are a water planet and as goes the ocean go we.

Based on my understanding of carbon footprints by income segment, higher-income segments, including the upper-middle class and the wealthy, consistently cause significantly more pollution and environmental damage than lower-income populations through their consumption patterns, lifestyle choices, and investments. In my opinion, it is unlikely that the working-class and low-income households are largely responsible for the overconsumption of costly seafood. Rather, I tend to think that the steady stream of demand and potential overconsumption of seafood likely come mainly from the upper-middle class and above. If so, perhaps they should consider helping to fund solutions.

For instance, in addition to enforcing tougher ocean environmental regulations on catch quotas and other measures designed to protect marine life, federal and state governments could levy excise taxes on all fishing-related items such as commercial and leisure fishing licenses, fishing tools, and seafood products. These excise taxes paid could then be returned to taxpayers in the form of tax deductions based on their income levels. Federal and state governments could also implement an additional 1.5% increase in income tax for individuals making over $125,000 and couples making over $250,000.

The collected tax revenue and fines would be reinvested into repairing environmental damage through ocean garbage removal and marine life restoration. Ultimately, however, this issue must be resolved on a global scale.

comments.body: It sounds like the most terrifying aspect might be that it is impossible for anyone to know what's actually going on. For both reader and characters, that inability to narrate oneself, one place in the world, in the world, is a fundamental, stabilizing, an existential need. Increasingly, we seem to know what's going on, climate change, societal polarization and authoritarianism, and an inability for the human species to adequately own up to these challenges. So the horror, perhaps, is that when the apocalypse comes, we no longer know what story to tell ourselves and we are truly adrift, aimless, and at the mercy, of our own decisions. The first New York ComiCon (NOT Comic Con!) was held in the early 1960s. In 1965, I ran off the program sheet on my Ditto spirit duplicator for Dave Kaler's ComiCon, held at the Hotel Broadway Central, with a press run of about 250, with some left over. 

This incarnation is a commercial venture, which makes a ton of money for someone. The comics fandom back then would find this incarnation of the convention nearly incomprehensible, I imagine.

comments.name: Sophie Marie
comments.body: I hate to be a Negative Nelly, but... I have attended NYCC since sometime in the late aughts, so probably 15 cons or so. I have to say, in my experience at NYCC in particular, this was one of the most poorly run events I've attended. It was clearly oversold, as there wasn't a panel or event that wasn't closed before most of the interested patrons could navigate their way through the Javits' crowd and labyrinthine hallways. Getting from a Level 1 panel to a Level 4 event in time to find an open door was nigh on impossible. Rooms weren't cleared following panels (e.g. the room wasn't cleared before the Godzilla Minus Zero panel -- SO many disappointed fans!), screwing it up for those who had been waiting for something they had their hearts set on. It was truly sad and too, too bad. The fun was sucked out of it for too, too many people.

At this class I weld pieces of metal together learning how the machines work, and what kind of welds there are. Though I do not want to do welding as a job, it will help me get into the career I want to do, which is to be a heavy machinery operator. This job requires multiple trades united into one which are mechanics, construction, welding, and having a CDL. In America young adults and teenagers are seeing that college is not their only option. Many people see that there is a lot of money in trades and are going into them, sometimes even leaving their white collar jobs just to join a trade. Going into a trade is not easy as it requires a lot of manual labor which is a reason many people leave or do not even think about joining. I think that going into a trade is really smart for young people who like to work with their hands, talk with other people, and make money.

As an Off Off Bway artist myself to read this article about the Irish Arts Center was so illuminating - and horrifying. So that's why I"ve never been able to raise money. You have to know and put together wealthy people with other wealthy people who you know are generous. Point is, if you have a very limited budget to begin with and so have little time to shmooze and raise money (most fundraisers are supported by family wealth) so it's a never-ending loop. Got money? Step this way? Despite the fact that it may be (probably is) you were drawn into the non-profit effort cuz it was far, far from the commercial pablum of Bway theater. (and believe me, the difference is palpable. I remember seeing Music Man as a guest of someone and it was the most choreographed, waiting for the laugh to come kind of experience). Not always, thank god - I went to see Stoppard's Leopoldstadt twice - but IMHO that's so rare. Anyway, I landed @ Theater for the New City years ago and if you do good work you could get up a play for the most limited budget around. (tho lately gender, racial and trans gender I.D. issues seem to be ascending) with all the baggage that that brings. In any case, may Crystal Field live to 150 cuz she still appreciates good work whatever it's slant. & the guy who ran the Roundabout was the same: Harvard MBA if memory serves - something like that. Sorry of this sounds so other worldly cuz indpndts are getting it in the neck.
